Where it began

Lance Klusener was born in Durban on 4 September 1971, and his boyhood was spent among the cane fields of a sugarcane farm near Empangeni. At primary school in Kwambonambi most of his classmates were Zulu, and he came away speaking their language so well that the nickname "Zulu" followed him for the rest of his career.

He was a late starter. At Durban High School he only made the first team in his final year, and after school came three years of military service. Natal's manager, Denis Carlstein, liked what he saw of his bowling and sent him to the provincial nets. There Malcolm Marshall, the great West Indian fast bowler, took him under his wing, and in 1993–94 he was in the Natal side.

The player

His Test debut came at Calcutta in 1996–97, and it began roughly: Mohammad Azharuddin once hit him for five fours in a row. Klusener answered in the second innings with 8 for 64, which would stay his best figures and which was long thought to be the finest return by a South African in a debut Test. In only his fourth Test, at Cape Town in January 1997, he came in at number nine and reached a hundred in 100 balls, then the quickest by a South African. In December 1999 he made 174 against England at Port Elizabeth.

In all he played 49 Tests between 1996 and 2004, scoring 1,906 runs at 32.86 with four hundreds and eight fifties, taking 80 wickets and holding 34 catches.

What made him special

In one-day cricket he was something new: a batsman who walked in late with a high, baseball-style backlift and simply cleared the ropes. The 1999 World Cup was his tournament. He was out only twice in eight innings, averaged 142.50, took wickets in every match bar one and was named Player of the Tournament. In the famous semi-final at Edgbaston he struck the first two balls of the final over for four to level the scores. The game ended in a tie and Australia went through, but nobody who watched forgot him. Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 2000.

If there was a gap in his game, it was that his Test wickets came at 37.91 each, a little dearer than that debut had promised. He made up for it by scoring runs at a rate most bowlers would happily have paid for.

Away from the middle

After his Test days he played county cricket for Northamptonshire from 2004, then turned to coaching. He ran the Dolphins, his old provincial side, from 2012 to 2016 and worked as Zimbabwe's batting coach. In September 2019 he became head coach of Afghanistan, and in his time there they won one of their three Tests. He also found time for fishing, and for commentary in both Zulu and Xhosa.

And finally

Plenty of all-rounders can talk a good game. Very few can do it in Zulu, Xhosa and English, and fewer had the runs to back up every word.
